data.title: Gap expands AI shopping with Alta Daily and new discovery tools
data.description:
Gap Inc. is pushing artificial intelligence (AI) deeper into how its shoppers discover and style its products.

The retailer on Monday unveiled new natural-language product discovery features for its Old Navy and Banana Republic brands. Separately, Gap said it’s launching an online styling experience with Alta Daily. The feature brings Gap’s namesake-brand merchandise into AI-generated outfit recommendations on the third-party styling app.

The announcements coincide with the retailer’s 30th anniversary of launching Gap Online in 1996. The company has been highlighting that milestone during this week’s SF Tech Week in San Francisco, framing AI as the next evolution in how customers shop its brands. Gap said it is also exploring emerging agentic commerce, in which AI can take actions on a shopper’s behalf.

“Thirty years ago, we launched gap.com, revolutionizing the way customers interacted with our brands, and today AI is creating a new opportunity to rethink how people shop for fashion,” Gap chief technology officer Sven Gerjets said in a statement.

Gap Inc., which owns Gap, Banana Republic, Old Navy and Athleta, ranks No. 20 in the Top 2000 Database. The database tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales and more.

Gap adds AI styling through Alta Daily

Rather than relying only on search boxes and product grids, Gap said it is experimenting with AI tools that can “increasingly understand intent, context and individual preferences.”

As part of that push, Gap is bringing its products into Alta Daily, the AI-powered digital closet and personal styling app. Shoppers can incorporate Gap-brand merchandise into personalized outfit recommendations and visualize the looks on their Alta avatars. The experience “brings AI-powered styling and discovery into a more visual and personalized environment,” Gap said.

To build their virtual wardrobes, Alta users can also digitize clothes they already own. From there, Alta says its app can generate outfits based on factors such as the user’s existing closet, personal style, schedule and weather.

That approach overlaps with the agentic-commerce model Gap says it has been exploring. Alta founder and CEO Jenny Wang told TechCrunch earlier this year that agentic commerce needs “a data layer that understands the shopper’s style preferences.” That data can include a shopper’s closet, past purchases and avatar, she said.

Meanwhile, shoppers can also find Gap Inc. products through Daydream, an AI-powered fashion platform that lets shoppers describe what they want in everyday language. Gap was already directing shoppers to the daydream.ing platform as a product-discovery option during the 2025 holiday season.

Old Navy and Banana Republic add AI tools

Gap is also reworking product discovery at Old Navy and Banana Republic around conversational AI. The tools let shoppers describe what they want in natural language and receive product ideas and recommendations.

Rather than translating an idea into keywords or filters, Gap said the AI tools are designed “to better understand customer intent and help people move more naturally from an idea to products that fit what they had in mind.”

Gap did not specify whether they are available through the brands’ websites, mobile apps or both.

Gap builds out AI strategy

The launches are part of a broader AI strategy Gap has been building across its ecommerce business. In 2024, the retailer established a dedicated Office of AI, focusing on “early use cases, primarily related to employee enablement,” Richard Dickson, Gap’s president and CEO, said at the time. Since then, the retailer has rolled out AI tools in customer service, personalized recommendations, fulfillment and other areas.

Gap is also directing some of its increased capital spending toward that work. During the company’s August earnings call, chief financial officer Katrina O’Connell said Gap’s capital expenditures will reach $650 million in fiscal 2026, up from $470 million last year. Some of those funds will flow into “the technology work that we’re doing around AI to be able to build capability,” she said.

Agentic commerce is a newer area for the company. In March, Gap became a launch partner for Bold Metrics’ Agent Sizing Protocol. By asking shoppers about fit and preferences, the technology helps conversational shopping agents determine the right apparel size.

At the same time, Gap announced support for Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol. The open standard, co-developed with Shopify, connects merchants with AI-powered shopping and checkout experiences. With the protocol, shoppers will be able to find and purchase Gap products using AI Mode in Google Search and in the Gemini app.

Gap was already bringing AI into the customer experience last year. Ahead of the 2025 holiday season, the retailer rolled out personalized recommendations and a digital assistant through the “Chat with Us” feature on its brands’ ecommerce sites and mobile apps.

Underlying many of those efforts is Gap’s partnership with Google Cloud. Launched in 2025, the partnership gives Gap access to Google technologies, including Gemini, Vertex AI and BigQuery.

data.title: TD Synnex, Siemens partner to expand industrial AI and IT-OT distribution globally
data.description:
TD Synnex and Siemens are set to collaborate internationally as the two companies partner on distribution.

Combining TD Synnex’s information technology offerings and Siemens’ own infrastructure and automation portfolio, the companies announced their agreement with their eyes on industrial use cases for artificial intelligence.

Together, they plan to meet demand for software and physical AI, according to Siemens.

Why TD Synnex and Siemens are working together

“With the incredible pace of change driven by AI, bringing IT and OT [operational technology] closer together has never been more important,” said Alastair Borissow, head of global distribution sales at Siemens. “By combining our established and highly capable global OT distribution network with TD Synnex’s complementary strengths in IT distribution, scale and ecosystem we intend to create new opportunities for our entire distribution channel.”

The Oct. 5 joint announcements noted that TD Synnex and Siemens agreed on a “joint framework” that would enable their global partnership. They highlighted Siemens’ technology and TD Synnex’s expertise and customer outcomes.

“IT and OT convergence is creating significant opportunities for partners to connect enterprise technology with the systems that power industries, infrastructure and buildings,” said Cheryl Day, senior vice president, new vendor acquisition and global solutions at TD Synnex. “By combining Siemens’ industrial technology expertise with TD Synnex’s global partner ecosystem, enablement capabilities and value-added services, we can help partners access new markets, develop new skills and address emerging opportunities in areas such as industrial AI, automation, cybersecurity and digital infrastructure.”

What TD Synnex and Siemens hope to achieve

“This is about far more than the distribution of technology — it is about connecting the industrial and IT worlds at unprecedented scale — by combining Siemens’ deep industrial technology with TD Synnex’s extraordinary reach across the global IT ecosystem — from hyperscalers and technology providers to thousands of specialist partners,” said Dion Smith, head of global partner ecosystem at Siemens. “We aim to create new routes to market, engage new buying centers within existing customers and reach entirely new customers, while accelerating the convergence of IT and OT.”

Smith noted the potential market that TD Synnex and Siemens could address through their combined efforts. In his view, the opportunity could be worth as much as $1 trillion. TD Synnex already operates across more than 100 countries, according to the distributor. If they are successful, Smith sees the partnership as a path to improve their reach.

“Together, we have the opportunity to unlock a trillion-dollar market and make secure industrial digitalization more accessible, scalable and impactful worldwide,” Smith stated.

data.title: Kroger launches a rewards Mastercard
data.description:
Grocery giant Kroger announced the launch of the Kroger Rewards World Elite Mastercard. The new co-branded credit card was built with the fintech company Imprint and Mastercard.

The card is designed to offer shoppers points at a rate of 5X their purchases, according to Kroger. Those purchases can be made through Kroger.com and the Kroger app.

In addition, the card fits within Kroger’s existing loyalty ecosystem. There, it will offer tiered rewards for fuel, in-store purchases, dining, and travel, plus a $100 welcome bonus.

Kroger’s leadership highlighted the company’s central ambitions when announcing the card.

Why Kroger is using the new Mastercard

“At Kroger, we’re always looking for new ways to help customers save,” said Megan Shaffer, group vice president of customer growth and strategy at Kroger. “From weekly grocery trips to filling up at the pump or paying bills, the Kroger Rewards World Elite Mastercard turns purchases into real savings. It is one more way we’re rewarding customers for the shopping they’re already doing.”

Imprint, the fintech platform powering the card’s technology, echoed the card’s diverse use.

“Kroger is one of America’s most trusted brands, with customer relationships built over decades of everyday shopping,” said Daragh Murphy, co-founder and CEO of Imprint. “Together, we set out to turn that loyalty into a card customers reach for every day, one that rewards the weekly Kroger trip and everything in between, with the modern, seamless experience they expect.”

Kroger ranks No. 7 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 2000 Database. The database ranks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales. Kroger is also No. 1 in the database’s Food & Beverage category. It also competes with Mass Merchants — Walmart and Target — that rank higher in the Top 2000 for online grocery sales.

The new card’s role for Kroger

Kiki Del Valle, executive vice president in charge of U.S. market development at Mastercard, expects the card to help remove friction from the buying process.

“Grocery spending is one of the most consistent and essential parts of life,” she assessed. “Together with Kroger and Imprint, we’ve created a seamless rewards experience that helps shoppers earn more on the purchases they already make, turning regular grocery trips into meaningful savings.”

Serhii Nikolaichuk, founder and CEO of The Capital Index, a technology development studio based in Austin, Texas, sees the card providing additional value to Kroger.

“This isn’t a credit card,” Nikolaichuk said. “It’s a delivery app with a bank attached.”

Nikolaichuk noted the richest point tiers are reserved for Kroger.com and app purchases up to 5X. That compares with up to 3X in-store. Combined with a free Boost delivery membership built into the Kroger app, the total offerings send a clear signal.

“Kroger is paying shoppers to move from the aisle to the screen, where it can see every basket and plan the next one.”

That shift is also the real story behind the fintech partnership, he said. With Imprint running the card and a bank issuing it behind the scenes, Kroger, not a big bank, owns the relationship. It will also control the data and the customer experience. The bank becomes plumbing. Amazon and Target already proved to grocers that the card can function as the loyalty program; now, Nikolaichuk said, that card lives inside the grocer’s own app.

“The bigger reason is coming next: AI shopping assistants,” Nikolaichuk said. “When an assistant builds the weekly cart, it will pay with whatever card is already on file, and it will follow the points.”

The grocer that owns the app, the card and the data owns the default, he said. In his view, the real prize is not the next swipe, but the next year of automatic reorders.

Kroger’s grocery competition

As for how Kroger’s approach stacks up against the approaches of its competitors, Nikolaichuk said Amazon and Target have trained shoppers to expect roughly 5% back. In that context, Kroger’s 5X sounds comparable on its face. But the points, Nikolaichuk says, are only as good as what they buy — fuel and groceries inside Kroger’s own ecosystem. For a loyal Kroger household that already fills up at Kroger gas stations, he said, that can beat a general cash-back card. However, for anyone who shops around, simple cash back may remain more straightforward.

“Kroger isn’t buying loyalty at the checkout,” he added. “It’s buying the default for the day an AI agent does the shopping.”

Still, Francesco Onorato, director of growth at Brandmovers, a loyalty and promotions marketing company, noted that Kroger is making a smart move by connecting its new store credit card with its loyalty program. He sees a key question in whether or not that will be enough in today’s competitive grocery and retail market.

“What’s interesting is that Kroger is focusing high-value incentives on orders made through the app and including free delivery as part of the offer,” Onorato posited. “This strategy uses payments as a means of guiding shoppers out of the aisles and into the digital channels. A reliable, engaging and personalized online shopping experience is going to be the true test of how their bet will pay off.”

data.title: Albertsons expands OpenAI work, adding enterprise ChatGPT use
data.description:
Albertsons Companies continues to explore how artificial intelligence (AI) best fits into its operations and ecommerce strategy, which now includes an expanded enterprise partnership with OpenAI and a ChatGPT plugin for the Safeway banner.

OpenAI detailed the companies’ latest work in a blog post on Oct. 1, noting that Albertsons’ teams were using ChatGPT to “navigate complexity, accelerate workflows and move promising ideas toward production faster.”

Albertsons is No. 17 in the Top 1000 Database. That database ranks the largest online retailers in North America by annual ecommerce sales.

OpenAI described the scope of its work with Albertsons as including ChatGPT Enterprise, in addition to what it referred to as “custom AI-powered experiences for its customers, data-driven recommendations and promotional insights built with the OpenAI API.”

Albertsons’ portfolio included more than 2,200 stores across its banners. Those banners encompass its namesake stores, Safeway, Vons, Jewel-Osco, Shaw’s, ACME and Tom Thumb.

Albertsons rolled out its Safeway plugin for ChatGPT in August.

“Research tells us that consumers are increasingly interested in using AI to help with grocery shopping,” said Jill Pavlovich, senior vice president, digital customer experience at Albertsons Companies, at the time. “By enabling our plugin in ChatGPT, we are making grocery shopping as simple as having a conversation by meeting our customers when and how they choose to shop.”

The plugin operates within the ChatGPT app experience. Once connected to ChatGPT and a shopper’s Safeway account, it enables a chat-style interface for planning grocery lists and making purchases.

Albertsons’ recent history of AI use

Previously, Albertsons became one of the first retailers to test ChatGPT’s ads in 2026. OpenAI welcomed the grocer, along with Target and Williams-Sonoma in the pilot, and its ads have continued to evolve alongside ChatGPT’s agentic commerce strategy throughout the year.

In addition to OpenAI, Albertsons has also worked with Google on an AI assistant experience. Notably, Albertsons was the first retailer to use Google Cloud’s conversational AI solution in 2025.

Looking ahead, OpenAI expects Albertsons to leverage its large language model to create internal predictive models, along with recommendations and insights about the grocer’s activities, thanks to employee tools, commerce-related apps and advertising solutions that OpenAI will power there.

data.title: Revelyst brands focus on discovery, understanding AI traffic
data.description:
Revelyst, which operates more than a dozen brands for outdoor recreation and related gear, has seen a rise in artificial intelligence-driven product discovery in 2026 — and it’s working to uncover what consumers are using AI platforms to understand about its products.

Consumers are learning more about Revelyst’s products outside of its brand sites, according to Tari Huddleston, global vice president of digital and ecommerce. Consumers are engaging with various AI tools — which can include ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity — to understand Revelyst products’ features and specifications.

“We’re seeing what the questions are that are being asked around our brand,” Huddleston told Digital Commerce 360. “Either their features or questions about the technology, the innovation that’s inside it. We’re watching that and seeing how that has changed. It’s not all transactional based anymore.”

Revelyst operates brands including:

  • Bell
  • Blackhawk
  • Blackburn
  • Bushnell
  • Bushnell Golf
  • CamelBak (No. 1,212 in the Top 2000 Database)
  • Camp Chef (No. 965 in the Top 2000)
  • Foresight Sports
  • Fox Racing
  • Giro
  • Primos
  • Quietkat
  • Simms
  • Stone Glacier

The Top 2000 Database ranks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Camp Chef is also No. 571 in Digital Commerce 360’s new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

AI discovery trends among Revelyst brands

Although Huddleston did not share specific metrics regarding AI referral traffic, she noted that her brands have seen comparable trends to other retailers Digital Commerce 360 has spoken with.

That is, retailers in early 2026 have seen about 1% to 3% of website traffic come from AI referrals. In the second half of 2026, that has risen to about 4% to 7%, but certainly less than 10% for those retailers.

Within that AI traffic subset, Huddleston noted, consumers shopping Revelyst brands are adding products to their carts more than their counterparts. The AI responses to their queries are leading them directly to product detail pages (PDPs) rather than homepages.

Such AI tools are helping consumers to complete the top-of-funnel product discovery, she said. That refers to the earliest stage of a consumer learning about a brand or its products.

“They’re ready to convert,” Huddleston said. “We’re seeing that they’ve done that homework and they’re ready to make that purchase.”

What consumers are using AI to understand about products

The rates of AI referrals to Revelyst brand sites are comparable to one another. AI traffic referrals are increasing among Revelyst brands, but they’re still small, according to Huddleston. She noted that “many other channels” are driving the majority of her brands’ traffic.

“I think the reason why it’s still small is because the discovery phase for the consumer, for our products, is not a short window,” Huddleston explained. “It’s not like someone’s deciding: Hey, I need a replacement of something — which is a quick purchase.”

Instead, it’s often a long-term investment, she said. Huddleston gave the example that a consumer shopping for a power sports helmet could be looking at a price range of $400 to $900 — “a sizable investment.”

That type of purchase often requires more research than smaller-ticket items. As a result, consumers are asking more questions about products to decide if they’re worth the price. Huddleston said Revelyst uses those questions to determine how it can improve its PDPs.

Another example was of a consumer asking about pads inside of a helmet and how speakers factored in.

“We would not have known that that was a feature that we need to call out and be able to make sure was searchable across the product unless we had been watching and seeing what type of conversations were happening inside the space,” Huddleston said.
